lede: Respiration is how a living cell gets the energy it needs out of food. Oxygen and glucose go in, energy comes out, and carbon dioxide and water are what is left. It runs in every cell, day and night, and a flask of sprouting peas warms up because of it.
can: Write the word equation with energy among the products.
Name the mitochondria as the organelle where respiration happens.
Give two uses of the released energy, and explain the boiled-pea control.

text: Aerobic respiration: the reaction every cell is doing right now

md: Every cell in you is doing this reaction right now, and it does not stop while you sleep. Glucose from your food meets oxygen from your breath, and the energy stored in the glucose is released for warmth, movement and growth. Carbon dioxide and water are left over.

alt: The word equation glucose plus oxygen gives energy plus carbon dioxide plus water, and beneath it the balanced symbol equation C6H12O6 plus 6O2 gives energy plus 6CO2 plus 6H2O, marked Higher Tier. A two-row table underneath contrasts photosynthesis, where energy sits on the arrow as a condition and the reaction is endothermic, with respiration, where energy is written as a product and the reaction is exothermic.

explain: Water. Three products, and CCEA writes 'energy' as the first of them — unlike photosynthesis, where energy goes on the arrow.

title: Why energy is written differently in the two equations
md: Photosynthesis **takes energy in**, so light is a condition that has to be supplied — it goes on the arrow. Respiration **gives energy out**, so CCEA writes energy among the products. That is the difference between **endothermic** and **exothermic** in one line of layout, and it is why 'energy' belongs in a box here and never in the photosynthesis equation.

prompt: Respiration is described as exothermic. What does that tell you?
explain: Exo means out. That is why a bag of germinating seeds warms up, and it is a Higher Tier clause in this outcome.

md: **Where, and how often.** Respiration happens in the **mitochondria**, in **every living cell**, **all the time** — plants included, day and night. It does not stop when you sleep and it does not stop in a leaf in the light. That last point is what the hydrogencarbonate-indicator questions in B1 are really testing.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Respiration"
why: Five minutes on aerobic respiration, the equation and why the reaction is exothermic. Watch it, then answer the question underneath without scrolling back.

prompt: In which organelle does aerobic respiration take place?
explain: The mitochondria. This clause is printed in bold in the specification, which marks it Higher Tier — but it is one word, so learn it either way.

text: What the energy is actually for

alt: A central circle labelled energy released with arrows to five boxes: heat to keep body temperature up, movement for muscles, growth to build new cells, reproduction, and active uptake or transport marked Higher.

md: The specification lists five: **heat**, **movement**, **growth**, **reproduction** and **active uptake/transport** (the last is Higher Tier). When a question says 'respiration releases energy — give two uses for that energy', it has already given you the release. The marks are for what the body spends it on.

title: Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q7 and B1 Higher Q2
md: The same QWC question ran on both tiers. Some answers had the carbon dioxide the wrong way round — **taken in rather than given out**. Others wrote that respiration releases energy, which the question had already told them; the marks were for **what the body does with it**. The scheme gave no top band without **at least one named use**.

prompt: A question asks for two uses of the energy released in respiration. Which answer earns both marks?
options: to produce energy, and to stay alive
explain: Two of the five named uses. 'To produce energy' repeats the question, and glucose and oxygen are the reactants, not uses.

title: PhET: Membrane Transport

task: Set up a concentration difference and watch particles diffuse down it. Then open a pump and move particles the other way. Write one sentence saying which of the two needs energy from respiration, and why.

alt: Two vacuum flasks each plugged with cotton wool and holding a thermometer. Flask A contains living germinating peas; flask B contains peas that were boiled and then cooled.

caption: Two flasks, one difference: whether the peas are alive.

md: Put germinating peas in a vacuum flask with a thermometer, and boiled (dead) peas in an identical one. After 3 days the living peas have warmed from 22.5 °C to 27.0 °C — a rise of 4.5 °C. The dead peas rose only from 22.5 °C to 22.8 °C, a rise of 0.3 °C. The living peas are respiring; the boiled ones cannot, so the extra 4.2 °C must come from respiration. That is the evidence that respiration is **exothermic**.

prompt: The living peas warmed from 22.5 °C to 27.0 °C. What was the temperature rise, in °C?
explain: 27.0 − 22.5 = 4.5 °C. Always give the rise, not the final reading.

title: Why flask B is not a waste of peas
md: Flask B is the **control**. It is identical in every way except that its peas are dead, so it shows that the temperature rise in flask A was caused by the **living** peas and not by the room warming up, the cotton wool or the flask itself. A control changes exactly one thing — and boiling the peas is how you change 'alive' without changing anything else.

prompt: Why were the peas in flask B boiled before the experiment?
options: To kill them, so they could not respire
To remove the water from them
answer: To kill them, so they could not respire
explain: Dead peas cannot respire, so flask B shows what happens with everything else the same and respiration removed.

md:
Write the **word equation**, with energy among the products.
Name the **mitochondria** as the site of the reaction.
Give **two uses** of the energy released.
Explain why living peas warm a flask and boiled peas do not.

Six to nine marks, and in most series this is the paper's six-mark QWC. Expect the word equation into boxes, the organelle named, two uses of the energy, and a data part on a temperature rise or a limewater result. Write **released**, never made: energy is not created. Stuck: write the equation out, because each box is a mark.
